answer_text:
Assume \(a<b\). We want a constant \(C\), independent of \(f\), such that

\[
\left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|\ge C\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt
\]

for every integrable \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\).

Consider the step function

\[
f(t)=
\begin{cases}
1, & a\le t\le \frac{a+b}{2},\\[2mm]
-1, & \frac{a+b}{2}<t\le b.
\end{cases}
\]

This function is integrable. Its integral is

\[
\int_a^b f(t)\,dt
=
\frac{b-a}{2}-\frac{b-a}{2}
=0,
\]

while

\[
\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt=b-a>0.
\]

If the desired inequality held for this \(f\), we would get

\[
0=\left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|
\ge C\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt
=C(b-a).
\]

Since \(b-a>0\), this forces

\[
C\le 0.
\]

Conversely, if \(C\le 0\), then for every integrable \(f\),

\[
C\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt\le 0\le \left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|,
\]

so the inequality holds.

Therefore, no positive universal constant exists. The largest possible constant is \(0\).

\[
\boxed{\text{No positive }C\text{ exists; the inequality holds for all }f\text{ exactly when }C\le 0.}
\]
